svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 3. Compartmentalization fails silently, and what to do about it
svg.desc: The top row shows why a boundary break produces no signal: nothing errors, no warning appears, the page works normally, and the damage is permanent from the moment it happens. The middle row gives three controls that produce a signal instead: make the windows visually distinct, pin sites to a container so the assignment is automatic, and keep a short incident log. The bottom band explains what to do after a break, because deletion does not undo it.
svg.text: Figure 3: Nothing Tells You When It Breaks
Every other control in this module reports failure. This one does not, which changes how you have to build it.

g.text: Nothing throws an error. The page loads exactly as it should.
No warning appears, because from the browser's view nothing went wrong.
You were signed in already, so it felt like convenience rather than a mistake.
The link is made in the first request. There is no window to catch it in.
Closing the tab does not unmake it. Deleting the cookie does not either.
The other party keeps its record regardless of what you do next.

svg.text: Three controls that produce a signal where the system gives none

g.text: A different theme, colour and window
position for every identity.
You cannot detect a boundary break
after the fact, so the only workable
control is one that stops you at the
moment before it.
Cheapest control in this lesson.
Pin each site to its container or
profile so the assignment happens
without you deciding.
A decision you make forty times a
day will eventually be made wrong.
A decision you made once will not.
Automate the routine cases.
One line per slip: what crossed,
which two identities, and what you
were doing at the time.
The log is not for guilt. It shows
you which boundary keeps failing,
so you can redesign that one.
Repeat slips are a design fault.

svg.text: After a break, treat it as disclosed rather than fixed

g.text: Clearing the cookie does not withdraw the record. Assume the link was made and decide what follows from that, which is a threat modeling question
from Lesson 1.4 rather than a browser question. If the identity was disposable, retire it and build a new one. If it was not disposable, work out what the
other party can now infer, and whether anyone has to be told. Then fix the boundary that failed, because it will fail the same way again otherwise.
